thread.title: Bank of America quietly raises visibility on LGBTQ issues with its LGBT-plus executive council

author: Mark Calvey
title: Bank of America quietly raises visibility on LGBTQ issues with its LGBT-plus executive council
text: – Senior Reporter, San Francisco Business Times Oct 29, 2018, 2:20pm PDT Bank of America has become more public in recent weeks about its LGBT-Plus Executive Leadership Council that was established in 2016 to boost the visibility of LGBTQ senior executives within the bank and in the community. Bank of America’s (NYSE: BAC) council now has 68 LGBT-plus executives, who are out and operating at the second or third level down from the CEO. Insiders say the day may not be far off that a direct report to the CEO could be LGBT-plus, a designation that's intended to emphasize the inclusion of all identities. Some might wonder why a council designed to boost LGBTQ visibility has been operating with a low public profile. But a focus on building internal support first is a common tactic in advancing LGBTQ equality in the workplace. “It’s not something we necessarily wanted to discuss externally yet. We wanted to get our feet wet, experience what we’ve been able to accomplish and develop the council’s purpose,” said Shelley Saraniti , a director with Bank of America Merrill Lynch in San Francisco and co-chair of the LGBT-Plus council. The fact that BofA is becoming more vocal about its LGBT-Plus Executive Leadership Council suggests the idea could soon spread more widely across corporate America. Even those who work closely with companies on diversity issues appeared surprised at the size of BofA’s LGBT-Plus council, much less that it even exists. “It takes a hell of a lot of courage to be an out executive,” said Jennifer Brown , a diversity-and-inclusion consultant, who said she’s not aware of any other company with such a council. After all, she points out, Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL) CEO Tim Cook is still the only out Fortune 500 chief executive. Some observers say out corporate executives, in some cases, have moved back into the closet as they rose through the ranks. The BofA council began with a steering committee of 10 executives, primarily on the West Coast. The council’s formation occurred as Salesforce.com (NYSE: CRM) CEO Marc Benioff and his counterparts at other companies were taking a public stance against laws permitting discrimination against the LGBT community that were under consideration in Indiana and Georgia at the time. When BofA’s council was established at the start of 2016, it had 34 members from nine states and three countries. Today, membership has doubled to 68 senior executives from 11 states and four countries. While the bank’s 32 chapters of its LGBT-Plus Pride Network include 26,000 out employees and their supporters, called allies, the bank’s LGBT-Plus Executive Leadership Council only includes out senior execs. Saraniti said the council’s internal visibility has provided a forum to address issues and questions affecting LGBTQ employees includes one manager asking how to handle any negative reaction from customers over a transgender employee transitioning in a politically conservative market. Saraniti said sometimes there’s an opportunity for what might best be described as teachable moments, such as the manager, who apparently never tuned in to an episode of “Modern Family,” asking another employee, “I thought you were gay. Why do you need parental leave?” But Saraniti said the LGBT-Plus Executive Council has been well supported by the bank’s C-suite. She noted that CEO Brian Moynihan has attended an annual gathering of the council in the past two years. For the most recent gathering he attended, Moynihan was scheduled to make a 15-minute appearance, but stayed an hour longer than that. Cathy Bessant , BofA’s chief technology and operations officer , is the senior management team’s non-LGBT liaison with the LGBTQ-Plus council. This month, the Financial Times named Bessant the top ally for LGBT workers as part of its annual OUTstanding LGBT-plus executives and allies. The LGBT-plus council fits with the bank’s lead it took on other LGBTQ workplace issues, including the adoption of policies and programs in 1983 to address employees with AIDS and the offering of domestic partner benefits in 1997, becoming the first financial institution to do so. Even then, the bank broadly defined domestic partners to expand it beyond the LGBT community in an effort to initially avoid customer backlash. The city of San Francisco required companies doing business with the city at the time to offer domestic partner benefits to its gay and lesbian employees. In a more recent move, Bank of America’s human resources office has expanded its concierge-like services for major life events, originally designed for employees taking a leave of absence, to include transgender employees transitioning. Meanwhile, other companies have moved in a different direction than Bank of America’s LGBT-plus council. Wells Fargo, for instance, has a companywide diversity-and-inclusion council that’s led by CEO Tim Sloan and includes a diverse mix of leaders. Since 2011, Wells Fargo (NYSE: WFC) has operated a leadership development program for “high-potential LGBT” employees. Back at Bank of America, Saraniti held a panel discussion this month at the bank’s San Francisco office urging LGBTQ employees to be comfortable being out at work. “We often hear, ‘It’s San Francisco. Why do we really need this here. It’s a progressive place to be. Don’t all of our employees feel comfortable?’ The answer is, ‘No, they don’t,’” Saraniti said. – Senior Reporter, San Francisco Business Times Oct 29, 2018, 2:20pm PDT Related Content
